questions.stem: A pressure of 142/76 mm Hg is charted. Which phase produces the upper value?
questions.rationale: The upper reading reflects arterial pressure during ventricular contraction.

questions.stem: What does the lower number in a brachial blood pressure reflect?
questions.rationale: The lower reading reflects arterial pressure during ventricular relaxation.

options.text: The difference between peak and minimum pressure
The pressure averaged across a cardiac cycle
Arterial pressure at peak ventricular contraction

questions.stem: A client's pressure changes from 126/74 to 148/74 mm Hg. Which calculated value rose by 22 mm Hg?
questions.rationale: Pulse pressure is systolic minus diastolic pressure, so a 22-point systolic rise with unchanged diastolic pressure raises pulse pressure by 22.

questions.stem: A sustained very rapid rhythm shortens the time between contractions. Which change can reduce stroke volume?
questions.rationale: A shortened diastolic interval leaves less time to fill and can reduce the volume ejected per beat.

options.text: Greater end-diastolic volume from slower cycling
Less time for the ventricle to fill

questions.stem: An increase in circulating volume raises ventricular end-diastolic stretch. Which term describes the changed load?
questions.rationale: Preload describes the stretch present before contraction. Afterload is the resistance encountered during ejection.

questions.stem: A patient develops marked systemic vasoconstriction. What ventricular load rises as the left ventricle ejects into the arterial system?
questions.rationale: Systemic vasoconstriction increases the resistance against which the left ventricle ejects.

questions.stem: The ventricle ejects 60 mL per beat at 80 beats/min. What is cardiac output?
questions.rationale: Multiply 60 mL by 80 beats/min to obtain 4,800 mL/min.

questions.stem: Heart rate rises from 60 to 90 beats/min while stroke volume falls from 90 to 60 mL. What happens to cardiac output?
questions.rationale: Both 60 × 90 and 90 × 60 yield 5,400 mL/min.

questions.stem: What measurement would establish whether more blood is pumped with each contraction?
questions.rationale: Stroke volume is measured per beat. Cardiac output is measured per minute.

questions.stem: Two clients have the same heart rate. Which variable explains why one has lower cardiac output?
questions.rationale: With identical heart rates, a lower stroke volume yields lower cardiac output.

questions.stem: Which history supports evaluating hypertension for a secondary cause?
questions.rationale: Kidney disease can cause secondary hypertension. Family history and age are risk factors for primary hypertension.

options.text: Blood pressure rose after development of kidney disease
Both parents had hypertension and no associated condition is known
Blood pressure increased gradually with age without another identified disorder
Family history and inactivity accompany longstanding hypertension

questions.stem: Which two characteristics can the client modify? Select exactly two.
questions.rationale: Tobacco exposure and activity level can change. Age and inherited risk cannot.

questions.stem: Which finding represents ocular target-organ damage in longstanding hypertension?
questions.rationale: Hypertension injures small retinal vessels, producing retinopathy.

questions.stem: Which situation most strongly suggests hypertensive emergency?
questions.rationale: Acute confusion suggests new target-organ dysfunction in the setting of severely elevated pressure.

options.text: Mildly elevated pressure after activity with no symptoms
Longstanding controlled pressure with stable chronic kidney disease
Markedly elevated pressure with new confusion
Markedly elevated pressure with baseline cognition and no acute organ injury

questions.stem: How does persistent hypertension promote vascular injury?
questions.rationale: Persistent pressure stresses the arterial wall and can damage its endothelial lining.

options.text: It decreases endothelial exposure to mechanical force
It increases mechanical stress on the vessel wall
It lowers pressure against the arterial lining

questions.stem: Why can a major fall in blood pressure threaten organ function?
questions.rationale: If arterial pressure falls too far, the pressure gradient driving organ blood flow may become inadequate.

options.text: Increased arterial pressure impairs vessel integrity
The rise in systemic pressure causes retinal injury

questions.stem: Which pair represents cerebral and renal target-organ complications, respectively?
questions.rationale: A TIA reflects transient cerebral ischemia, while chronic kidney disease reflects renal injury.

questions.stem: Which lunch selection best reflects a lower-sodium dietary approach for hypertension?
questions.rationale: Choosing fresh foods and avoiding added salt reduces sodium compared with cured, smoked, or packaged options.

options.text: Unsalted roasted chicken with fresh vegetables

questions.stem: Which complications in a patient with chronic uncontrolled hypertension affect the heart? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Heart failure, infarction, and dysrhythmias involve the heart. Retinopathy affects the eye, and a TIA affects the brain.

questions.stem: Why can hypertension due to coarctation be classified as secondary?
questions.rationale: Aortic coarctation is an identifiable structural contributor, which supports classification as secondary hypertension.

options.text: It is defined by an isolated elevated reading
It is classified solely by whether symptoms occur
A specific underlying structural cause is identifiable
Its severity is determined by family history alone

questions.stem: Which change initiates the described sequence of atherosclerosis?
questions.rationale: Endothelial injury precedes lipid deposition. Rupture and thrombosis are later complications.

questions.stem: Where does oxidized LDL accumulate early in plaque formation?
questions.rationale: Oxidized LDL accumulates in the innermost arterial layer, the intima.

questions.stem: Which cell takes up oxidized LDL and becomes a foam cell?
questions.rationale: Macrophages ingest oxidized LDL and become foam cells.

questions.stem: Which change directly adds extracellular matrix to the developing plaque?
questions.rationale: Smooth muscle cells migrate into the intima and secrete matrix, including collagen.

options.text: Smooth muscle migration and matrix secretion
Loss of all smooth muscle from the vessel wall

questions.stem: Which plaque feature makes rupture more likely?
questions.rationale: A thin cap is more vulnerable to rupture than a thick, intact cap.

questions.stem: A coronary plaque ruptures. Which immediate event can abruptly obstruct blood flow?
questions.rationale: Rupture exposes thrombogenic material, allowing a clot to form at the site.

options.text: Improved flow through the disrupted site
Slow expansion of the vessel lumen

questions.stem: A plaque gradually enlarges without rupturing. Why can downstream tissue still become ischemic?
questions.rationale: As plaque grows into the lumen, it can restrict downstream flow even before rupture.

options.text: The plaque increases the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity
The plaque enlarges only outside the vessel lumen
The plaque narrows the lumen and limits flow
The plaque increases the lumen and lowers resistance

questions.stem: Which two factors are modifiable risks for atherosclerosis? Select exactly two.
questions.rationale: Tobacco exposure and blood lipids can be modified. Age and inherited risk cannot.

questions.stem: Which explanation connects chronic high arterial pressure to plaque development?
questions.rationale: Mechanical stress from elevated pressure can injure the endothelial lining and promote plaque formation.

options.text: Mechanical stress can injure the endothelium
Pressure protects the endothelium from disruption
Pressure prevents LDL from accumulating in the intima
Pressure stops inflammatory cells from entering the vessel wall

questions.stem: Put the early events leading to a fatty streak in order.
questions.rationale: Endothelial injury precedes LDL deposition. Macrophages take up oxidized LDL, become foam cells, and accumulate as a fatty streak.

questions.stem: Calf pain develops at a reproducible walking distance and subsides after stopping. What best explains it?
questions.rationale: Exercise raises muscle oxygen demand. When narrowed arteries cannot increase supply, pain develops and eases when demand falls at rest.

options.text: Arterial flow rises beyond muscle demand
Arterial supply cannot meet exercising muscle demand
Venous valves close excessively during walking
Skeletal muscle pumping stops during exercise

questions.stem: Which pair most strongly favors arterial insufficiency in a client with leg discomfort?
questions.rationale: A cool foot and weak pulse support reduced arterial inflow. Edema and varicosities more strongly suggest venous disease.

options.text: Pitting edema and intact pedal pulses
Ankle swelling and brown skin discoloration
Cool foot and weak pedal pulse

questions.stem: A foot turns pale when elevated and red when dependent. Which explanation fits this pattern?
questions.rationale: A poorly perfused limb can become pale when elevated and red when lowered.

options.text: Normal pulses rule out a vascular cause
Impaired arterial perfusion produces position-dependent color change
Effective venous valves prevent blood from returning to the heart

questions.stem: Which action directly activates the calf muscle pump?
questions.rationale: Calf contraction compresses leg veins and helps propel blood toward the heart.

options.text: Repeated ankle movement and calf contraction

questions.stem: What causes elevated pressure in leg veins with incompetent valves?
questions.rationale: Valve incompetence allows backflow, pooling, and elevated venous pressure.

options.text: Increased forward flow through competent valves

questions.stem: Which change suggests progression beyond intermittent claudication?
questions.rationale: Tissue necrosis suggests advanced ischemia. Reproducible pain that resolves with rest is consistent with claudication.

options.text: Pain that consistently resolves with rest
Return of normal foot color after warming

questions.stem: Which wound pattern most strongly supports arterial insufficiency?
questions.rationale: Distal tissue loss with a cool foot and weak pulses points to impaired arterial inflow. Edematous ankle wounds favor venous disease.

options.text: Irregular gaiter-area wound with dependent swelling
Distal toe ulcer with weak pulses and a cool foot
Shallow medial ankle ulcer with edema and palpable pulses
Weeping ankle wound with brown discoloration and warmth

questions.stem: Which finding cluster best fits chronic venous insufficiency?
questions.rationale: Dependent swelling and discoloration with palpable pulses favor venous congestion.

options.text: Distal toe necrosis, absent pulse, cold skin
Exercise-induced calf pain with diminished distal pulses
Dependent edema, brown ankle discoloration, palpable pedal pulse
Cool foot, weak pulse, elevation pallor

questions.stem: Which two findings support reduced distal arterial perfusion? Select exactly two.
questions.rationale: Delayed refill and a diminished distal pulse suggest poor arterial perfusion.

questions.stem: What is the normal function of one-way venous valves when calf muscles relax?
questions.rationale: Venous valves limit retrograde flow between calf contractions.

options.text: They stop all blood from reaching the heart
They direct blood into the leg arteries
They increase arterial resistance during relaxation
They prevent blood from falling back down the leg

questions.stem: Imaging shows localized dilation involving all layers of an artery. What is this finding?
questions.rationale: A true aneurysm includes all vessel-wall layers. A pseudoaneurysm is a contained leak outside the disrupted vessel wall.

questions.stem: After an arterial puncture, blood collects outside the arterial wall in a contained pocket. What best classifies it?
questions.rationale: A contained arterial leak outside the vessel wall is a pseudoaneurysm.

questions.stem: A client describes abrupt severe tearing pain from the chest to the back. Which process fits this pattern?
questions.rationale: An intimal tear can allow pressurized blood to separate aortic wall layers, causing abrupt severe pain.

options.text: A stable aneurysm slowly expands without wall separation
Blood enters an inner aortic tear and tracks between wall layers
A chronic venous valve leak raises pressure in leg veins
A plaque gradually reduces flow to an exercising calf

questions.stem: What is the false lumen in aortic dissection?
questions.rationale: The dissection creates a second channel between layers of the wall.

options.text: A dilated segment containing all wall layers
A narrowed lumen caused by chronic plaque
A new channel formed between layers of the aortic wall
The original passage through the aorta

questions.stem: Which two histories increase risk for aortic aneurysm? Select exactly two.
questions.rationale: Chronic hypertension and smoking are listed risk factors.

questions.stem: Which finding may occur with an unruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm?
questions.rationale: An abdominal aortic aneurysm may cause a pulsating abdominal sensation or remain asymptomatic.

questions.stem: What is the direct consequence if an aortic aneurysm ruptures into surrounding tissue?
questions.rationale: Rupture lets blood escape into adjacent tissue or a body cavity and can cause major blood loss.

options.text: Increased blood return to the heart

questions.stem: Which inherited condition is listed as a risk for aortic dissection?
questions.rationale: Marfan syndrome affects connective tissue and is a risk factor for dissection.

questions.stem: Which study is identified as the gold standard for defining a suspected acute aortic dissection when feasible?
questions.rationale: CT angiography can define the dissection and its extent. The other tests cannot map an aortic false lumen.

questions.stem: Why is blood pressure control a goal in medical management of aortic disease?
questions.rationale: Reducing arterial pressure reduces the mechanical load on the aortic wall.

options.text: It widens the false lumen to restore flow
It increases the pressure distending the aneurysm
It reduces mechanical stress on the aortic wall
It increases shear stress at the injured site

questions.stem: Chest pressure predictably occurs uphill and stops with rest. Which diagnosis best fits?
questions.rationale: Predictable exertional pain that resolves with rest is characteristic of stable angina.

questions.stem: Chest pain begins at rest with transient ST depression and serial troponins remain negative. Which diagnosis fits best?
questions.rationale: Rest pain suggests unstable ischemia, and persistently negative serial troponins support angina rather than infarction in this scenario.

questions.stem: A client with acute chest pain has a rising troponin and ST depression. Which classification fits?
questions.rationale: A rising troponin with ischemic symptoms and without ST elevation supports NSTEMI.

questions.stem: A client has ischemic chest pain, diagnostic ST elevation, and rising troponin. Which diagnosis fits?
questions.rationale: Diagnostic ST elevation in the setting of ischemic symptoms supports STEMI.

questions.stem: What produces symptoms in angina?
questions.rationale: Angina occurs when myocardial oxygen supply is insufficient for demand. Infarction involves myocardial injury and cell death.

options.text: A temporary mismatch between myocardial oxygen supply and demand
Myocardial cell death after prolonged ischemia
Impaired ventricular filling from fluid around the heart

questions.stem: Which two data sources together best help differentiate infarction from angina? Select exactly two.
questions.rationale: ECG changes characterize the ischemic pattern, while serial troponins help detect myocardial injury.

questions.stem: Which findings can accompany acute MI? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Sweating, nausea, and dyspnea can accompany acute MI. Chronic skin changes and reproducible calf pain are peripheral vascular cues.

options.text: Reproducible calf pain relieved by rest

questions.stem: A client develops a new unstable ventricular rhythm after an infarction. What best explains the new complication?
questions.rationale: Ischemic and injured myocardium can alter conduction and trigger a ventricular dysrhythmia.

options.text: The infarct increases conduction uniformity throughout the ventricle
Venous valve failure causes the ventricular rhythm change
Pericardial fluid improves ventricular electrical stability
Injured myocardium can disrupt electrical conduction

questions.stem: After MI, a client becomes hypotensive with cool extremities. What mechanism explains cardiogenic shock?
questions.rationale: Loss of pumping capacity after MI can cause inadequate cardiac output and systemic hypoperfusion.

options.text: The damaged heart cannot generate adequate forward flow
Venous valve failure prevents local calf drainage
Arterial plaque increases blood delivery to the tissues
Improved cardiac contraction causes excess perfusion

questions.stem: Match each pattern to its chest-pain classification.
questions.rationale: The pattern of symptoms, ECG findings, and troponin distinguishes the four classifications.

pairs.prompt: Rest pain with negative serial troponins

questions.stem: An echocardiogram shows fluid surrounding the heart within the pericardial sac. What does this finding describe?
questions.rationale: An effusion is excess fluid in the sac surrounding the heart.

source.name: 3140_7_Disorders of Cardiac Function, Heart Failure and Circulatory Shock.pdf

questions.stem: Why can a smaller, rapidly developing effusion be more dangerous than a larger, gradual one?
questions.rationale: The pericardium can stretch over time. Rapid accumulation can raise pressure substantially even with less fluid.

options.text: Slow accumulation always produces higher pressure at a smaller volume
Pressure depends exclusively on total fluid volume
The pericardium has less time to stretch and accommodate the fluid
Rapid accumulation gives the pericardium more time to stretch

questions.stem: Which change directly limits cardiac output in tamponade?
questions.rationale: Rising pressure outside the chambers restricts filling and reduces stroke volume.

source.name: 3140_7_Disorders of Cardiac Function, Heart Failure and Circulatory Shock.pdf

options.text: Venous valves increase preload without obstruction

questions.stem: Which auscultatory finding is consistent with fluid around the heart?
questions.rationale: Fluid surrounding the heart can dampen heart sounds.

options.text: A fixed split second heart sound

questions.stem: Why is new hypotension in a patient with an enlarging effusion concerning?
questions.rationale: Hypotension can reflect a fall in cardiac output from compression of the heart.

options.text: The effusion may be compressing the heart and impairing output
The effusion is likely increasing stroke volume
The effusion demonstrates improved systemic perfusion
The effusion typically raises effective circulating volume

questions.stem: Which findings in a client with a known effusion are consistent with hemodynamic deterioration? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Hypotension, tachycardia, and worsening dyspnea can accompany compression and impaired output.

source.name: 3140_7_Disorders of Cardiac Function, Heart Failure and Circulatory Shock.pdf

questions.stem: Which type of shock can result when pericardial pressure prevents adequate filling?
questions.rationale: Tamponade mechanically obstructs cardiac filling, producing obstructive shock.

questions.stem: Which development would explain an effusion following pericardial inflammation?
questions.rationale: Pericardial inflammation can increase fluid in the surrounding sac.

source.name: 3140_7_Disorders of Cardiac Function, Heart Failure and Circulatory Shock.pdf

options.text: Inflammation traps fluid only within the pleural space
Inflammation increases arterial blood volume within the ventricles
Inflammation promotes fluid accumulation in the sac
Inflammation drains fluid from the pericardial sac

questions.stem: What makes tamponade different from an uncomplicated effusion?
questions.rationale: Tamponade develops when pericardial pressure impairs cardiac function.

source.name: 3140_7_Disorders of Cardiac Function, Heart Failure and Circulatory Shock.pdf

options.text: The fluid moves into the ventricular myocardium
The fluid produces an arterial plaque rupture
The fluid creates pressure sufficient to impair cardiac function
Any measurable fluid automatically produces hemodynamic compromise

questions.stem: Arrange the events in the progression from an enlarging effusion to impaired perfusion.
questions.rationale: Accumulating fluid raises external pressure, limits filling, and reduces output.

source.name: 3140_7_Disorders of Cardiac Function, Heart Failure and Circulatory Shock.pdf

options.text: Fluid accumulates in the pericardial sac
External pressure on the heart rises

questions.stem: Where is the primary infection in infective endocarditis?
questions.rationale: The infection affects the inner cardiac surface and often involves a valve.

questions.stem: Why does injecting drugs with nonsterile equipment increase endocarditis risk?
questions.rationale: Injecting with nonsterile equipment can introduce organisms directly into the bloodstream.

options.text: Organisms can enter the bloodstream and seed a valve
The injection causes LDL deposition in the valve
Increased venous pressure dissects the aorta
The injection increases ventricular afterload directly

questions.stem: What explains increased infective endocarditis risk in a client with a prosthetic valve?
questions.rationale: A prosthetic surface can provide a site where circulating organisms adhere and grow.

options.text: The valve directly raises pressure in the pericardial sac
Circulating organisms can adhere to the prosthetic surface
Prosthetic valves produce transient coronary vasospasm
Prosthetic valves lower the oxygen-carrying capacity of blood

questions.stem: Which new finding with persistent fever supports evaluating for valve involvement?
questions.rationale: A new regurgitant murmur can reflect a valve that is no longer closing effectively.

options.text: An isolated widened pulse pressure at baseline

questions.stem: What causes an embolic complication of left-sided infective endocarditis?
questions.rationale: Fragments of infected vegetations can enter the systemic arterial circulation from the left heart.

options.text: Venous pooling forces blood through arterial valves
A thickened valve cap breaks open inside the arterial intima
Material breaks off a vegetation and travels into systemic circulation
Pericardial fluid enters systemic arteries through intact myocardium

questions.stem: The nurse reviews the provider order exhibit for a client with fever and suspected infective endocarditis. Which statements correctly explain the purpose of the orders? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Cultures can identify the organism. Echocardiography evaluates valve structure and can detect vegetations or regurgitation. Neither test provides the other test’s result.

options.text: Blood cultures can identify an organism in the bloodstream.
Echocardiography can evaluate a valve for a vegetation.
Blood cultures measure the severity of valve regurgitation.
Echocardiography identifies the species of the bloodstream organism.

exhibit.title: Provider orders
exhibit.text: Obtain blood cultures. Obtain echocardiogram to evaluate the valves.

questions.stem: A client with a left-sided vegetation develops sudden unilateral weakness. Which complication explains the change?
questions.rationale: A left-sided vegetation can embolize to a cerebral artery and produce focal neurologic findings.

questions.stem: Which two findings are classic peripheral clues to infective endocarditis? Select exactly two.
questions.rationale: Osler nodes are tender. Janeway lesions are typically painless.

questions.stem: Match the lesion or process to its description.
questions.rationale: The lesions differ in tenderness and location. A vegetation remains attached until material breaks away and embolizes.

targets.text: Detached material carried to a distant artery
Infected material attached to a valve
Painless lesions on palms or soles
Tender lesions on fingers or toes

questions.stem: A client with known tricuspid valve endocarditis develops septic emboli. Which destination follows the path of blood leaving the right heart?
questions.rationale: Blood leaving the right ventricle enters the pulmonary arteries, where right-sided septic emboli can lodge.

questions.stem: Which mechanism explains reduced ejection fraction in systolic heart failure?
questions.rationale: Reduced contractility decreases the fraction of filled ventricular volume ejected.

source.name: 3140_7_Disorders of Cardiac Function, Heart Failure and Circulatory Shock.pdf

options.text: Improved contractility increases the fraction ejected
Increased filling always normalizes the fraction ejected
Weak ventricular contraction reduces the fraction ejected
Impaired relaxation alone maintains the fraction ejected

questions.stem: Why can a client with diastolic heart failure have a preserved ejection fraction?
questions.rationale: Ejection fraction is a ratio. A normal ratio can coexist with low filling volume and impaired relaxation.

source.name: 3140_7_Disorders of Cardiac Function, Heart Failure and Circulatory Shock.pdf

options.text: A preserved fraction establishes normal filling
Impaired relaxation always causes an increased end-diastolic volume
Preserved ejection fraction proves absence of congestion
A stiff ventricle can eject a normal fraction of a smaller filled volume

questions.stem: Which symptom specifically describes orthopnea?
questions.rationale: Orthopnea is breathlessness when recumbent. Waking from sleep breathless describes paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea.

source.name: 3140_7_Disorders of Cardiac Function, Heart Failure and Circulatory Shock.pdf

options.text: Breathlessness when lying flat that improves upright
Sudden waking from sleep with breathlessness
Breathlessness that occurs only when standing

questions.stem: A client with left-sided failure develops bilateral crackles. What mechanism explains this?
questions.rationale: Left-sided dysfunction can raise pressure in the pulmonary circulation, resulting in congestion and crackles.

source.name: 3140_7_Disorders of Cardiac Function, Heart Failure and Circulatory Shock.pdf

options.text: Pressure backs up into the pulmonary circulation
Pressure backs up primarily into the leg veins
Low pressure in pulmonary capillaries pulls fluid into alveoli
Systemic venous congestion first causes isolated ankle edema

questions.stem: Which findings favor systemic venous congestion in right-sided failure? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Jugular venous distension, liver enlargement, and dependent edema reflect systemic venous congestion.

source.name: 3140_7_Disorders of Cardiac Function, Heart Failure and Circulatory Shock.pdf

questions.stem: Which lab test listed on the course worksheet supports ventricular wall stress in suspected heart failure?
questions.rationale: BNP rises in response to myocardial wall stretch and can support the assessment of suspected heart failure.

questions.stem: Which change links chronic hypertension to development of heart failure?
questions.rationale: The ventricle works against higher arterial pressure over time, increasing workload and promoting dysfunction.

source.name: 3140_7_Disorders of Cardiac Function, Heart Failure and Circulatory Shock.pdf

options.text: High arterial resistance improves forward flow
Sustained pressure load makes the ventricle work harder

questions.stem: Why can a previous myocardial infarction lead to systolic failure?
questions.rationale: Infarction can reduce the amount of myocardium available to generate contractile force.

source.name: 3140_7_Disorders of Cardiac Function, Heart Failure and Circulatory Shock.pdf

options.text: Scar tissue increases the strength of ventricular contraction
The infarct increases the amount of viable muscle
Loss of viable muscle reduces pumping strength

questions.stem: A client has jugular venous distension, edema and pulmonary crackles. What pattern best explains the combination?
questions.rationale: Jugular venous distension and edema indicate systemic congestion, while crackles suggest pulmonary congestion.

source.name: 3140_7_Disorders of Cardiac Function, Heart Failure and Circulatory Shock.pdf

options.text: Isolated systemic congestion with clear lungs
Isolated pulmonary congestion without systemic signs
Impaired arterial flow confined to the legs

questions.stem: A ventricle holds 120 mL before systole and ejects 36 mL. What is its ejection fraction?
questions.rationale: Ejection fraction is 36 mL divided by 120 mL, or 30%.

source.name: 3140_7_Disorders of Cardiac Function, Heart Failure and Circulatory Shock.pdf

questions.stem: Which calculation yields BMI for an adult whose weight is recorded in kilograms?
questions.rationale: BMI uses kilograms and meters squared.

options.text: Weight divided by height in meters squared
Weight divided by height in meters

questions.stem: A 72-kg adult is 1.80 m tall. What is the BMI to one decimal place?
questions.rationale: 72 divided by 3.24 equals 22.2.

questions.stem: Which measure estimates the energy used to sustain basic functions at rest?
questions.rationale: BMR describes resting energy needs for basic functions.

questions.stem: A client consistently consumes more energy than they expend. What trend follows if the imbalance persists?
questions.rationale: A sustained energy surplus increases stored energy.

options.text: Stable weight due to equal energy balance

questions.stem: A client wants to understand why activity can influence weight even if food intake stays constant. Which explanation fits?
questions.rationale: Movement is a component of total energy expenditure.

options.text: Activity changes height in the BMI formula
Activity is excluded from energy balance
Activity automatically lowers basal energy needs

questions.stem: Two clients have identical BMI values. Which conclusion is supported by BMI alone?
questions.rationale: BMI reports a ratio and cannot distinguish fat from lean mass.

options.text: Their weight relative to height squared is the same
They have the same body fat percentage
They have the same resting energy needs
They have the same daily caloric intake

questions.stem: Why can two adults of the same weight have different basal metabolic rates?
questions.rationale: Lean tissue contributes to resting energy use.

options.text: Resting energy use measures food intake
Differences in lean tissue can alter resting energy use
Weight fixes basal energy use at a single value
Height is the only determinant of resting energy use

questions.stem: Match each adult BMI value to its category.
questions.rationale: Adult categories are under 18.5, 18.5–24.9, 25–29.9, and 30 or greater.

questions.stem: An adult gains weight while height remains unchanged. What happens to BMI?
questions.rationale: At fixed height, BMI changes in the same direction as weight.

options.text: It remains constant because height is unchanged
It cannot be calculated without BMR
It rises because the numerator increases
It falls because the numerator increases

questions.stem: Which two variables determine whether stored body energy tends to increase or decrease? Select exactly two.
questions.rationale: The difference between intake and expenditure determines energy balance.

questions.stem: A client describes sour fluid rising into the mouth. What process explains the sensation?
questions.rationale: Gastric contents move backward into the esophagus and can reach the mouth.

options.text: Reflux of gastric contents into the esophagus
Passage of bile into the duodenum
Retention of stool in the colon
Movement of food from esophagus into stomach

questions.stem: Which normal barrier limits backward flow from the stomach?
questions.rationale: The lower esophageal sphincter is the barrier at the gastroesophageal junction.

questions.stem: Which history best supports GERD over an isolated reflux episode?
questions.rationale: Recurrent bothersome symptoms support a disease pattern.

options.text: A brief change in stool consistency
One brief episode after an unusually large meal
A single bout of nausea during travel

questions.stem: A client’s burning retrosternal discomfort is worse when lying down after eating. What explains the position effect?
questions.rationale: Gravity assists clearance when upright.

options.text: Recumbency increases gravity-assisted drainage into the stomach
Recumbency stops contact between gastric contents and esophagus
Recumbency reduces gravity-assisted clearance of refluxate
Recumbency closes the lower esophageal sphincter more tightly

questions.stem: How can elevated abdominal pressure promote reflux?
questions.rationale: A larger pressure gradient favors retrograde flow when the barrier is weak.

options.text: It blocks acid production by the stomach
It speeds clearance of acid from the esophagus
It increases the pressure driving stomach contents toward the esophagus

questions.stem: Which tissue change can follow repeated exposure to refluxed acid?
questions.rationale: Repeated acid exposure can inflame esophageal mucosa.

questions.stem: Which pattern best distinguishes regurgitation from vomiting?
questions.rationale: Regurgitation can occur without the forceful contractions of emesis.

options.text: Gastric contents rise with little or no forceful retching
Gastric contents are expelled with repeated abdominal contractions
Abdominal contractions continue after gastric contents are expelled
Contents move from the esophagus into the stomach

questions.stem: Which two processes can increase esophageal acid exposure? Select exactly two.
questions.rationale: A weak barrier permits reflux and slow clearance prolongs contact.

questions.stem: What is Barrett esophagus in the context of long-standing reflux?
questions.rationale: Chronic reflux can lead to metaplasia of the distal esophageal lining.

options.text: A gallstone lodged in the cystic duct
A change in the distal esophageal lining associated with chronic injury
A perforation of the duodenal wall
An inflammatory lesion limited to the ileum

questions.stem: A client with chronic reflux develops progressive difficulty swallowing. Which complication can explain it?
questions.rationale: Healing after repeated injury can produce an esophageal stricture.

options.text: Excessive dilation of the esophagus from acid clearance
Increased width of the esophageal lumen
Increased relaxation of the ileocecal valve

questions.stem: A client uses NSAIDs regularly and develops a gastric ulcer. Which effect explains the risk?
questions.rationale: NSAIDs reduce prostaglandin synthesis, which can impair mucus and bicarbonate defenses.

options.text: Enhanced bicarbonate delivery to the stomach surface

questions.stem: Which organism is associated with chronic gastric inflammation and peptic ulcers?
questions.rationale: H. pylori can promote chronic gastritis and ulceration.

questions.stem: Where are common peptic ulcers located?
questions.rationale: Gastric and duodenal ulcers affect upper GI sites exposed to acid and pepsin.

questions.stem: Which mechanism allows ulcer injury to persist?
questions.rationale: Acid and pepsin injure tissue when protection is impaired.

options.text: Acid and pepsin contact tissue after mucosal defenses fail
Excess mucus shields exposed tissue from acid
Increased bicarbonate neutralizes gastric acid at the ulcer
Repaired mucosa restores an intact barrier

questions.stem: A client with an ulcer develops black, tarry stools. What complication is suggested?
questions.rationale: Digested upper GI blood typically produces black tarry stool.

options.text: Upper GI bleeding with digestion of blood

questions.stem: A client with known PUD develops abrupt generalized pain and a rigid abdomen. Which complication fits?
questions.rationale: A full-thickness defect lets irritating gastric contents reach the peritoneum.

options.text: Mild constipation with intact bowel wall
A contained mucosal erosion without leakage
Perforation with irritation of the peritoneum

questions.stem: A bleeding ulcer causes lightheadedness on standing. Which mechanism explains the symptom?
questions.rationale: Blood loss reduces effective circulating volume and can cause orthostatic symptoms.

options.text: Increased red cell mass slows cerebral blood flow
Reduced gastric motility lowers venous pressure directly
Loss of circulating volume reduces perfusion on standing
Increased albumin draws fluid into vessels

questions.stem: Which pain location fits the usual description of ulcer discomfort?

questions.stem: An older client with type 2 diabetes has glucose 728 mg/dL, high serum osmolality and minimal ketones. Which condition best fits?
questions.rationale: Marked hyperglycemia and hyperosmolality with minimal ketosis fit HHS.

questions.stem: Select exactly two findings that favor DKA over HHS.
questions.rationale: Significant ketonemia and the resulting acidosis distinguish DKA. Both states can cause glucosuria and dehydration.

questions.stem: Put the events in order from severe insulin deficiency to the respiratory response in DKA.
questions.rationale: Severe insulin deficiency promotes lipolysis and ketogenesis. The resulting metabolic acidosis triggers compensatory ventilation.

options.text: Ketone acids accumulate and bicarbonate falls
Deep rapid breathing compensates for acidosis
Fat breakdown supplies fatty acids to the liver
